source.title: Analyzing limits for in-context learning
source.authors: Omar Naim; J'erome Bolte; Nicholas Asher

record.tranche_reason: The paper mentions induction heads as a prior proposal but does not test or rely on induction-head formation or function. Its experiments concern polynomial function-prediction ICL, not induction behavior or the claimed loss-curve transition.
record.gate_note: The induction-head statement is cited in related work. The paper's own polynomial ICL results do not measure heads, token-index loss, induction behavior, or training-time formation; those results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: Induction heads appear only in related work, citing Olsson et al., and in one remark that the two-layer result corroborates prior findings. The experiments measure MSE on synthetic polynomial regression in context. They never examine heads, previous-token composition, copying, loss by token index or training dynamics, so no version is tested. 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses'.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that transformers do not implement classical learning algorithms in context. ICL instead relies mainly on memorization and interpolation within the training distribution, and out-of-distribution failure is architectural (attention, layer normalization). They support this with a proof for attention-only models on linear functions.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the induction-head method; it evaluates polynomial function prediction in context.
record.method_sensitivity: Polynomial ICL performance varies with training and test distributions; the paper also reports differences across training schemes and with versus without layer normalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Polynomial ICL in 2L and 12L models is near-zero error in-distribution but degrades sharply under coefficient shift (e.g. σ=10 gives MSE about 28–46).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On synthetic regression ICL, in-distribution accuracy does not transfer to substantially shifted inputs or coefficients.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors state two-layer attention-only models are necessary and sufficient for in-distribution polynomial ICL, and that one-layer models fail. No one-layer numbers are tabulated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At least two attention layers are needed for in-context regression, consistent with but not testing a composition-based mechanism.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing layer normalization eliminates boundary values and lowers in-distribution error, but does not fix out-of-distribution error (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer normalization causes bounded-output extrapolation failures in ICL regression.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: What Can(’t) Transformers Do?
record.problems: The experiments use controlled synthetic mathematical functions rather than natural-language tasks; the paper states that the models are relatively modest in size, up to 38M parameters. The reported results do not include error bars or statistical tests.
record.rows_left_out: Additional numerical results in Tables 1–5 and Figures 1–4 concern polynomial prediction, training-distribution width, training schemes, or layer normalization. They were not separately entered because they do not measure induction behavior or the claimed training-time transition.

untested.parts: No previous-token heads, head composition, or [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying measured.
No training-time tracking of head formation, ICL gain or loss bump.
No measure of induction heads' share of ICL; no large models.
No induction-head detection across models, families or modalities.
Training distributions vary, but only regression error is measured, not induction-head formation.
No identification of which heads carry few-shot learning.

record.verdict_notes: Relation corrected from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The only link to induction heads is the two-layer necessity remark citing Olsson et al., with no head-level analysis.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure previous-token heads, head composition, or copying [A][B] … [A] → [B].
Does not track induction-head formation, training-time loss bumps, or token-index ICL gains.
Does not measure induction heads or their contribution to most ICL in large transformers.
Does not assess induction behavior across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Varies training and test distributions for polynomial ICL, but does not measure whether or when induction heads form or relate their formation to ICL persistence.
Does not identify mechanisms or heads carrying few-shot task learning, or compare those mechanisms with induction heads.
Does not track induction formation or assess whether it comprises separate transitions.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformers
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated polynomial-function prediction in context when training and test distributions match.
rows.baseline: Least-squares prediction is described as the comparison; exact baseline value not stated.
rows.value: Near-zero prediction error; comparable to classical polynomial regression methods such as Least Squares.
rows.note: This is a result about polynomial function-prediction ICL, not induction-head behavior.
rows.check: Polynomial-regression ICL error, not induction behaviour. Table 1 models are 2L8AH; the 'attention-only' framing comes from the text. The values are near-zero at σ=1 and rise to about 39–46 at σ=10. Least squares is the reference, but no baseline number is given.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1; Table 1: 2L8AH models have squared error 0.00 at σ=1; accompanying text describes near-zero in-distribution error and performance comparable to least squares.

rows.subject: transformer models trained on polynomial functions
rows.size_stated: Relatively modest model sizes, up to 38M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated polynomial-function prediction under shifts in input or coefficient distributions.

conditions.value: deviates significantly from the training distribution

rows.baseline: Performance when test and training distributions closely match; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Prediction errors increase substantially; the text says performance deteriorates significantly under sufficiently large shifts.
rows.note: The paper also reports that moderate expansion of the training range can improve generalization, while extremely broad training distributions degrade performance.
rows.check: Not an induction measure. Subjects are 12L8AH models (Table 2) and degree-1 models trained at varying widths (Table 3). The 'up to 38M parameters' size is borrowed from cited Naim and Asher 2024 and the limitations section; it is not stated for these runs. Table 3 varies training-distribution width, a different condition from the test shift.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.1–4.2; Tables 2–3: distribution shifts increase prediction errors; moderate training widths improve generalization, while extremely broad training degrades accuracy.

relation.reason: The paper cites induction heads in related work and links its two-layer result to Olsson et al.; it neither examines induction heads nor uses them as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: Polynomial-regression prediction errors do not measure induction behavior, head composition, training phase changes, or induction heads' causal contribution to in-context learning.

source_check.notes: At σ=10, Table 1 reports MSE 39.17–46.47 for 2L8AH models; Table 2 reports 27.85–37.66 for 12L8AH models. These support the synthesis's rounded range but concern polynomial regression, not induction-head behavior.
